topics: 🍞 Torah-Law Blessings — Grace after Meals from 'you shall eat and be satisfied'; the Torah blessing from 'when I proclaim the Lord's name'
🔁 Rabbi Yoḥanan's Kal VaḤomer — deriving after-Torah and before-food blessings, and why it is refuted
❓ Doubt About Shema — Rav Yehuda: don't repeat Shema (rabbinic) but repeat emet veyatziv (Torah); Rabbi Elazar disagrees
🛑 Already Prayed? — Shmuel: stop even mid-blessing; join a congregation only if you can add something new
🔟 Entering Mid-Amida — finish before Modim (Rav Huna) or before Kedusha (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi); kedusha needs ten
📜 Does Rabbi Yehuda Expound Juxtaposed Verses? — the sorceress, the father's skirt, and the ba'al keri at Horeb

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Torah Law, Rabbinic Law, and Doubt
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 21a–21b
overview.hebrewSource: קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, וּתְפִלָּה דְּרַבָּנַן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Why may a ba'al keri contemplate Shema and recite Grace after Meals, yet not begin the Amida? Because Shema and Grace are Torah law while prayer is rabbinic. That distinction drives the whole daf: Rav Yehuda derives the Torah sources for Grace and for the blessing over Torah; Rabbi Yoḥanan's attempt to extend them by kal vaḥomer is refuted. The Torah/rabbinic line then decides what to do in cases of doubt — repeat Shema? repeat prayer? — and what to do if you remember mid-Amida that you already prayed. Rav Huna and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi dispute whether a latecomer must finish before Modim or before Kedusha, which turns on whether an individual may say kedusha alone. Finally the Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda can let a ba'al keri recite blessings, given the Sinai juxtaposition — and traces his approach to expounding adjacent verses.

slides.title: 🍞 Which Blessings Are Torah Law?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yehuda's two sources, and Rabbi Yoḥanan's attempt to double them

boxes.title: From the Torah
items: Blessing before Torah: כִּי שֵׁם ה׳ אֶקְרָא הָבוּ גֹדֶל לֵאלֹהֵינוּ (Deut. 32:3)

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan's kal vaḥomer
items: Food needs no blessing before, yet needs one after — Torah, which needs one before, surely needs one after
Torah needs no blessing after, yet needs one before — food, which needs one after, surely needs one before

boxes.title: Refutation (תְּיוּבְתָּא)
items: Food is special: one derives bodily pleasure
Torah is special: it gives eternal life
And the mishna says the ba'al keri blesses after food but not before — so the before-food blessing is not Torah law

callout.label: Why this matters here:
callout.text: Prayer lacks the acceptance of Heaven's yoke? So does Grace after Meals, yet the ba'al keri recites it. The real line: Shema and Grace are Torah law; prayer is rabbinic.

slides.title: ❓ In Doubt — Repeat or Not?
slides.subtitle: The Torah/rabbinic distinction decides every case of uncertainty
rows: Does not repeat — Shema is rabbinic; 'when you lie down' refers to Torah study (Abaye to Rav Yosef)
Repeats — it commemorates the Exodus, a Torah obligation
Does not repeat — prayer is rabbinic
Repeats: if only a person would pray all day long!

callout.label: Objection to Rav Yehuda:
callout.text: If emet veyatziv is Torah law, the ba'al keri should recite it after Shema! Answer: its point is the Exodus, already mentioned in the tzitzit paragraph of Shema. Then say emet veyatziv and skip Shema? Shema is preferable — it has both the Exodus and the yoke of Heaven.

slides.title: 🛑 Remembering Mid-Prayer That You Already Prayed
slides.subtitle: Two rulings of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and why both are needed

nodes.content: 📜 Shmuel: one standing in prayer who remembers he already prayed stops, even in the middle of a blessing
❓ But Rabba bar Avuh told Rav Naḥman that students who began a weekday blessing on Shabbat must complete that blessing!
✅ No comparison: on Shabbat he is truly obligated in all eighteen blessings — the Sages merely spared him in honor of Shabbat. Here he has already prayed
📜 Shmuel again: one who prayed and enters a synagogue mid-prayer may pray again only if he can introduce something new

columns.label: Why the 2nd ruling?
columns.content: Without it: an individual vis-à-vis a congregation might count as one who has not prayed

columns.label: Why the 1st ruling?
columns.content: Without it: one who already began might be allowed to continue

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: A rabbinic prayer already discharged has no further claim — unless something genuinely new is added.

slides.title: 🔟 Walking In While the Congregation Prays
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna vs. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and the source that kedusha needs ten

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: If he can begin and finish before the prayer leader reaches Modim, he begins; if not, he does not.

lines.speaker: R' Yehoshua b.L.
lines.text: If he can begin and finish before the leader reaches Kedusha, he begins; if not, he does not.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The dispute: one holds an individual may say kedusha on his own; the other holds an individual may not say kedusha alone.

lines.speaker: Rav Adda b.A.
lines.text: The source: וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Leviticus 22:32) — any matter of sanctity requires no fewer than ten.

lines.speaker: Rabbenai
lines.text: Gezera shava 'among'–'among': 'Separate yourselves from among this congregation' (Numbers 16:21), and 'this evil congregation' — the ten spies (Numbers 14:27). Just as there ten, so here ten.

lines.speaker: Everyone
lines.text: Whatever the ruling, one does not interrupt the Amida to respond to kedusha.

lines.speaker: Rav Dimi
lines.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, students of Rabbi Yoḥanan: one interrupts for nothing except 'May His great name be blessed' — even mid-Ma'aseh Merkava. But the halakha does not follow this.

slides.title: 📜 Rabbi Yehuda and Juxtaposed Verses
slides.subtitle: How can Rabbi Yehuda let a ba'al keri recite blessings, given the Sinai juxtaposition?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: 'impart them to your children' (Deut. 4:9) is next to 'the day you stood at Horeb' (4:10) — just as those with emissions were barred at Sinai, so they are barred from Torah
2️⃣ Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda doesn't expound juxtapositions (סְמוּכִים)? Rav Yosef: even one who doesn't expound them elsewhere does so in Deuteronomy

3️⃣ Proof he doesn't elsewhere: ben Azzai derives stoning for a sorceress from its neighbor 'lies with a beast' (Exodus 22:17–18). Rabbi Yehuda: shall we execute someone because of juxtaposition? Rather, from medium and wizard (Lev. 20:27)
4️⃣ Proof he does in Deuteronomy: he forbids a woman raped by one's father — 'shall not uncover his father's skirt' (Deut. 23:1) sits beside the rape law (22:29)
5️⃣ Answer: he needs the Horeb juxtaposition for a different teaching — one who teaches his son Torah is as if he received it at Horeb

6️⃣ Mishna: a zav with an emission and similar cases need immersion; Rabbi Yehuda exempts. But he exempts only a zav (unfit for immersion anyway) — a plain ba'al keri he obligates, so his 'blesses' must mean something narrower (continued on the next daf)

summary.principle: Whether an obligation is Torah law or rabbinic law determines who must fulfill it, whether it is repeated in doubt, and whether one may stop in the middle.

flowSteps.content: 🍞 Grace after Meals (Deut. 8:10) and the blessing before Torah (Deut. 32:3) are Torah law; Rabbi Yoḥanan's kal vaḥomer to extend them is refuted
❓ Doubt: Rav Yehuda — don't repeat Shema (rabbinic), repeat emet veyatziv (Torah); Rabbi Elazar — repeat Shema, not prayer; Rabbi Yoḥanan — pray all day
🛑 Shmuel: remembered you already prayed? Stop even mid-blessing; join a congregation only if you can add something new

columns.content: 🔟 Latecomer: finish before Modim (Rav Huna) or Kedusha (R' Yehoshua b. Levi) — kedusha needs ten, from 'among'
📜 Rabbi Yehuda expounds juxtapositions in Deuteronomy but uses Horeb for 'teaching a son = receiving at Horeb'

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Shema and Grace are d'oraita, prayer is d'rabbanan — so a ba'al keri contemplates Shema and blesses after food, but need not begin the Amida

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara conclude that a ba'al keri may contemplate Shema and recite Grace after Meals, but need not begin the Amida?
o: Because prayer lacks the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven
Because Shema and Grace after Meals are Torah law, while prayer is rabbinic
Because prayer is too long to recite in a state of impurity
Because the community is not engaged in prayer
quiz.e: The 'yoke of Heaven' answer failed because Grace after Meals also lacks it; the Gemara settles on the Torah/rabbinic distinction.

quiz.q: Why is Rabbi Yoḥanan's kal vaḥomer deriving a Torah-law blessing before food refuted?
o: Because Torah study gives eternal life, which food does not, and the mishna says the ba'al keri does not bless before food
Because the blessing before food was instituted by Ezra
Because food is eaten more often than Torah is studied
Because Rav Yehuda's verse contradicts it
quiz.e: Torah is special in providing eternal life, so its before-blessing cannot be transferred to food; and the mishna's ruling that the ba'al keri blesses after but not before food shows the before-food blessing is only rabbinic.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda, one who is unsure whether he recited Shema does not repeat it, but one unsure about emet veyatziv does. Why?
o: Emet veyatziv is shorter
Shema is rabbinic but emet veyatziv, commemorating the Exodus, is Torah law
Emet veyatziv contains the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven
Shema may only be recited once per day
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda holds that 'when you lie down and rise' refers to Torah study generally, so Shema is rabbinic and doubt is treated leniently, while remembering the Exodus is a Torah obligation treated stringently.

quiz.q: What is the underlying dispute between Rav Huna (finish before Modim) and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (finish before Kedusha)?
o: Whether Modim or Kedusha is more important
Whether a latecomer must pray with the congregation at all
Whether an individual may recite kedusha on his own
Whether the prayer leader must repeat the Amida
quiz.e: Rav Huna holds an individual may say kedusha alone, so he need only reach Modim with the congregation; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds kedusha requires the congregation, so he must finish before it.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara explain that Rabbi Yehuda does expound juxtaposed verses in Deuteronomy, yet does not derive the ba'al keri prohibition from 'the day you stood at Horeb'?
o: He rejects the authority of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
He uses that juxtaposition to teach that one who teaches his son Torah is as if he received it at Horeb
He holds a ba'al keri is never prohibited from Torah
He derives the prohibition from the sorceress instead
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda needs the same adjacent verses for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's other teaching about teaching one's son, so they are unavailable for the ba'al keri derivation.
